t.4.53.1: While Tāra, whose splendor equaled that of the moon, lord of the stars, was speaking thus, Hanumān then thought that the kingdom had been seized by Aṅgada.
t.4.53.2: Hanumān regarded the son of Vālin as endowed with intelligence of eight aspects, possessed of the four kinds of strength, and having the fourteen virtues.
t.4.53.3: Him, continually being filled with energy, strength and valour, and growing in splendour like the moon at the beginning of the bright fortnight.
t.4.53.4: Him who was equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect and like his father in valour, and who listened dutifully to Tāra as Puraṃdara did to Śukra.
t.4.53.5: Then Hanumān set about winning over Aṅgada, who was learned in all the śāstras and was worn out from toiling in his master's cause.
t.4.53.6: Expounding the third of the four means of policy, he sowed dissension among all those vānaras by the excellence of his speech.
t.4.53.7: When they had all been won over and divided, he then frightened Aṅgada with many fearsome words, joined with anger as a means of persuasion.
t.4.53.8: You, O Tāreya, are more capable in battle than your father; truly you are able to bear firmly the burden of the kingdom of the monkeys, just as your father did.
t.4.53.9: For monkeys are ever fickle of mind, O bull among monkeys; without you, and parted from their sons and wives, they will not endure being commanded.
t.4.53.10: For these will not call you to account, I tell you this plainly to your face, neither this Jāmbavān, nor Nīla, nor the great monkey Suhotra.
t.4.53.11: For neither I nor all these others can be drawn away from Sugrīva by you, whether by conciliation, gifts and the other such means, or by force.
t.4.53.12: They say that even holding one's ground, once a weak man has quarrelled with a stronger, brings him ruin. Therefore the weak, mindful of protecting himself, should not make war.
t.4.53.13: This place that you regard as a protecting nurse is known to be merely a cave; for Lakṣmaṇa's arrows, splitting it open would be a trifling task.
t.4.53.14: Indra did but little when he hurled his thunderbolt long ago; Lakṣmaṇa with his sharpened arrows would split it open like a cup of leaves. And Lakṣmaṇa has many iron shafts of that kind.
t.4.53.15: The very moment you settle down here, O scorcher of foes, all the monkeys, firm in their resolve, will give up their lives.
t.4.53.17: Bereft of your friends and of your kinsmen who wish you well, you will become sorely frightened even of a quivering blade of grass.
t.4.53.16: Remembering their sons and wives, ever anxious and hungry, and worn out by sleeping on wretched beds, they will turn their backs on you.
t.4.53.18: And the terrible arrows of Lakṣmaṇa, of mighty speed and irresistible, would never fail to strike you, seeking to slay you once you have turned away.
t.4.53.19: But when you have gone back together with us and presented yourself humbly, Sugrīva will, in due order of succession, establish you in the kingdom.
t.4.53.20: Your paternal uncle is devoted to dharma and wishes for your affection. He is firm in his vows, pure and true to his promises, and he will never seek to kill you.
t.4.53.21: He wishes only to please your mother, and his very life is devoted to her; and he has no other offspring, so, Aṅgada, let us go.
